html:
1Core Concepts and Definitions

Stakeholder (PMBOK 8 glossary): an individual, group, or organization that may affect, be affected by, or perceive itself to be affected by a decision, activity, or outcome of a portfolio, program, or project.

Stakeholder engagement: the activities conducted to identify and analyze stakeholder needs and manage expectations and communications to foster stakeholder support.

Fact Detail
Who Internal or external; individuals, groups or organizations; a project may have a handful or potentially millions
Attitude Supportive, neutral, or opponents — effective engagement covers all three, not just supporters
Changes over time Different stakeholders in different phases; their power, influence and interest shift as the project unfolds
Cadence Identification, prioritization and engagement are reviewed and updated routinely, at least at each phase
Skills Interpersonal and leadership skills with stakeholders matter "just as important, if not more so" than technical PM skills; the two named key skills are negotiation and conflict management
Link Closely tied to communications management (Topic 20)

Examples of stakeholders (PMBOK 8 Figure 2-31): suppliers and vendors, customers, end users, regulatory bodies, local communities, family; sponsor, governing bodies, PMO, steering committees; project manager, project management team, project team.

Exam angle

a person who only feels affected is still a stakeholder, and "low power" never means "ignore" (regulators and communities can stop a project).

Six key concepts of the domain

Concept Key points
Sponsor engagement Sponsors hold decision-making authority, secure resources and keep the project aligned with strategy. Typical sponsor activities: initiate the project and define objectives and business case; approve the charter and its changes; assign and empower the PM; set up a steering committee and sit on it; approve the project management plan and its changes; ensure long-term benefits realization; propose termination; authorize completion. An active sponsor is a critical success factor.
Stakeholder satisfaction Prioritized and built into project objectives. Driven by continuous communication to understand needs, address issues as they occur, manage conflicting interests and involve stakeholders in decisions.
Team engagement Team members are critical stakeholders and are treated as such; the work, and the recommendations for hard decisions, come from them.
Communications management Tailor communication to each stakeholder so they have what they need to decide and know the risks of an action (Topic 20).
Data-driven decision-making Secure timely stakeholder decisions by preparing solid supporting material and guiding the decision process. AI tools (predictive analytics, data visualization) can help present fact-based recommendations.
Vendor and supplier management Vendors are stakeholders wherever external resources are used (Topic 22).

2The Stakeholder Engagement Processes

PMBOK 8 groups seven processes in the Stakeholders domain. This file covers the four engagement processes; the three communications processes (Plan Communications Management, Manage Communications, Monitor Communications) are in Topic 20.

Process Focus area Purpose and key benefit Key outputs Decision tools
Identify Stakeholders Initiating Identify stakeholders and analyze/document their interests, involvement, interdependencies, influence and potential impact. Benefit: the right focus for each stakeholder or group. Continuous identification acts as a risk management strategy. Performed periodically. Stakeholder register; change requests; updates to requirements, communications, risk and engagement plans; assumption log, issue log, risk register Stakeholder analysis, stakeholder mapping, questionnaires/surveys, brainstorming, document analysis, expert judgment, meetings
Plan Stakeholder Engagement Planning Develop strategies to engage stakeholders based on their needs, expectations, interests, requirements and potential impact. Benefit: an actionable plan for interacting effectively. Periodic. Stakeholder engagement plan; project management plan updates Stakeholder engagement assessment matrix, prioritization/ranking, root cause analysis, assumption and constraint analysis, benchmarking, mind mapping
Manage Stakeholder Engagement Executing Communicate and work with stakeholders (including collaborating with sponsors) to meet needs and expectations, address issues and foster appropriate involvement. Benefit: more support, less resistance. Throughout. Change requests; updates to communications plan, engagement plan, change log, issue log, lessons learned register, stakeholder register Communication skills and feedback; interpersonal skills (conflict management, cultural awareness, negotiation, observation/conversation, political awareness); ground rules; meetings
Monitor Stakeholder Engagement Monitoring & Controlling Assess how effective engagement is, find needed adjustments and refine strategies. Benefit: keeps engagement efficient and effective as the project and environment change. Throughout. Work performance information; change requests; updates to plans and registers Stakeholder analysis, alternative analysis, root cause analysis, multicriteria decision analysis, voting, assessment matrix, feedback, presentations, active listening, leadership, networking

3Identifying, Analyzing and Categorizing Stakeholders

(ECO Task 4: identify and analyze stakeholders · Task 5: categorize stakeholders)

3.1 Where stakeholders are found

Project charter, business case, benefits management plan, agreements/contracts, requirements documentation, issue and change logs, EEFs and OPAs. Techniques: questionnaires/surveys, brainstorming, document analysis, meetings with experts.

3.2 What stakeholder analysis records

A list of stakeholders with: position in the organization, role on the project, their stake, expectations, attitude (level of support) and interest in project information.

PMBOK 8 names five kinds of stake:

Stake Meaning
Interest Affected by a decision related to the project or its outcome
Rights Legal or moral (e.g., occupational health and safety law; protecting heritage sites or the environment)
Ownership Legal title to an asset or property
Knowledge Specialist knowledge, or knowledge of the organization's power structures
Contribution Funds or other resources, or intangible support such as advocacy and acting as a buffer against organizational politics

3.3 Stakeholder register (a project document, kept alive)

Block Content
Identification Name, organizational position, location and contact details, role on the project
Assessment Major requirements, expectations, potential to influence outcomes, phase of the life cycle where they have most influence or impact
Classification Internal/external; impact/influence/power/interest; upward/downward/outward/sideward; or any model the PM chooses

3.4 Mapping and categorizing models

Model What it does Best for
Power/interest, power/influence, impact/influence grids Group stakeholders by authority (power), concern about outcomes (interest), ability to influence outcomes (influence) or to cause changes to planning/execution (impact) Small projects or simple stakeholder relationships
Stakeholder cube Combines the grid elements into a three-dimensional model Richer pictures of the community; helps communication strategy
Salience model Classes by power, urgency (need for immediate attention: time-constrained or high stakes) and legitimacy (involvement is appropriate). Adaptation: proximity replaces legitimacy for team-level analysis Large, complex stakeholder communities; ranking relative importance
Directions of influence Upward, downward, outward, sideward (see below) Seeing where pressure comes from
Prioritization Rank stakeholders and their requirements; top = highest interest and influence. Methods: MoSCoW, 100-point method, cost of delay, Kano analysis Many stakeholders, changing membership, complex relationships

Quadrant strategies for the grid [Beyond PMBOK 8 — standard exam wording]:

Quadrant Strategy
High power, high interest Manage closely (partner, involve in decisions)
High power, low interest Keep satisfied (consult on key decisions, don't overload)
Low power, high interest Keep informed (regular updates, listen for input)
Low power, low interest Monitor (minimum effort; watch for change)

Beyond PMBOK 8 The salience model's seven classes appear in some exam material: dormant (power only), discretionary (legitimacy only), demanding (urgency only), dominant (power + legitimacy), dangerous (power + urgency), dependent (legitimacy + urgency), definitive (all three).

4Engagement Levels and the Assessment Matrix

(ECO Task 4: plan engagement and optimize alignment of stakeholder needs, expectations and project objectives)

Level Meaning
Unaware Unaware of the project and its potential impacts
Resistant Aware of the project and impacts, but resists the changes; unsupportive of the work or outcomes
Neutral Aware, neither supportive nor unsupportive
Supportive Aware of the project and impacts, and supportive of the work and outcomes
Leading Aware, and actively engaged in making the project a success
  • C = current engagement; D = desired engagement (the level the team judges essential for project success).
  • The gap between C and D directs how much communication and engagement effort the stakeholder needs.
  • Closing that gap is an essential element of monitoring stakeholder engagement.
  • Not everyone must be "Leading": set D by what the project needs from that stakeholder.

5The Stakeholder Engagement Plan (SEP)

  • A component of the project management plan that identifies the strategies and actions needed to promote productive stakeholder involvement in project decisions and execution.
  • Can be formal or informal, detailed or broadly framed, depending on project needs and stakeholder expectations.
  • Beyond PMBOK 8 In practice it records current vs desired engagement levels and the approach for each individual or group.
  • It is periodically updated (every phase, whenever monitoring shows a gap or the stakeholder set changes).
Stakeholder engagement plan Communications management plan
Answers How do we get each stakeholder to the engagement level we need? What information goes to whom, when, how, and by whom?
Driven by Stakeholder register, assessment matrix Stakeholder communication requirements
Relationship Drives and stays consistent with the communications plan Operationalizes the engagement strategy for information flow

6Engaging Stakeholders in Practice (Executing the Plan)

(ECO Task 4: execute the stakeholder engagement plan · analyze and tailor communication · build trust and influence)

What Manage Stakeholder Engagement looks like: ongoing two-way communication, addressing concerns before they become issues, negotiating, managing conflict, working with the sponsor, confirming agreements, and updating the change log, issue log, lessons learned register and stakeholder register.

Skills PMBOK 8 names for this work

Skill Key points
Influencing Often needed with no direct authority (matrix). Key abilities: persuasion, clearly articulating positions, active listening, awareness of different perspectives, gathering information to reach agreement while maintaining mutual trust
Negotiation A discussion aimed at reaching agreement. Used to win support, resolve conflicts, reach consensus on needs; can build trust and harmony
Political awareness Recognizing formal and informal power relationships; knowing the organization's strategies, who holds power and influence, and being able to communicate with them
Cultural awareness Understanding differences between individuals, groups and organizations and adapting the communication strategy to reduce misunderstanding
Active listening Acknowledging, clarifying, confirming, understanding and addressing barriers; essential in global or cross-cultural settings
Emotional intelligence Identify, assess and manage your own emotions and those of others and of groups; reduces tension and increases cooperation
Facilitation Guiding a group to a decision with full participation, mutual understanding and buy-in
Networking Relationships inside and outside the organization to exchange information and gain stakeholder support
Conflict management Address early, usually in private, with a direct and collaborative approach (Topic 26)

Building trust (ECO enabler) Beyond PMBOK 8practical behaviors

Be transparent (bad news early), keep commitments, listen before responding, involve stakeholders in decisions that affect them, treat everyone fairly and respectfully. These mirror the PMI Code of Ethics values of honesty, fairness and respect (Topic 06).

Tailoring communication to stakeholder needs (ECO enabler)

Choose method and detail by stakeholder: email for formal updates, instant messaging for quick questions, feedback loops, face-to-face for sensitive topics; adjust detail to role; multilingual updates and virtual forums for global audiences. A global virtual team usually needs collaboration tools with clear documentation. Details in Topic 20.

7Aligning and Managing Expectations

(ECO Task 5: identify expectations, facilitate alignment, mentoring · Task 6: internal and external customer expectations, satisfaction)

Step What the PM does Tools
1. Identify expectations Ask internal customers (sponsor, functional managers, team, PMO) and external ones (customers, end users, regulators, suppliers, communities) Interviews, questionnaires/surveys, focus groups, observation/conversation (job shadowing), customer talks and tests, document analysis
2. Categorize and prioritize Group stakeholders; rank their requirements Grids, salience, MoSCoW, 100-point method, Kano
3. Facilitate alignment Make assumptions, constraints and success criteria explicit; bring conflicting parties together to agree; document the agreement Facilitation, negotiation, workshops, ground rules
4. Align and maintain outcomes Keep deliverables and measures consistent with the agreed expectations; route new asks through change control Reviews/demos, requirements traceability, change control
5. Monitor satisfaction and respond Collect feedback, gauge satisfaction, adjust the engagement strategy Feedback, surveys, Net Promoter Score, trend in change requests, issue log

Key ideas

  • A project can meet scope, schedule and budget and still fail on expectations. Satisfaction is part of the project objectives.
  • Unspoken or conflicting assumptions (e.g., "no interruption to service" vs "a planned outage window") must be surfaced and agreed before baselining.
  • Coaching vs mentoring (ECO enabler: organize and act on mentoring opportunities):
Coaching Mentoring
Purpose Help a person find the solution to a specific problem on their own by asking the right questions Counsel and guide by sharing knowledge, skills and experience
Time horizon Goal-oriented, specific Long-term, ongoing relationship
Format One-to-one One-to-one

Typical uses: mixing seniority levels in the team so juniors get mentoring (PMBOK 8 Standard §2.5.1.2), coaching a new product owner or sponsor in adaptive ways of working, helping a resistant stakeholder understand change.

Early signals and what to do with them Beyond PMBOK 8exam practice

Scenario questions often hide a small signal. The best answer usually responds directly to the people involved (meet, ask, re-engage) rather than reviewing documents, analyzing patterns first, or sending more information.

Signal or situation Best response
Delivery matched the signed plan, but a partner or customer says their expectations were not met Acknowledge the gap and engage them on what remains; do not re-argue what the plan said
Informal remarks about quality or service; no formal complaint Treat them as an early satisfaction signal: meet the person and understand the concern
Stakeholders stopped contributing because earlier input went nowhere Rebuild trust by showing how their input shapes the outcome before asking for more
A community or group trusts another party (for example a contractor) more than the owner Involve the trusted party in engagement instead of spending time proving the owner's case
Overall satisfaction scores are stable, but key accounts stop attending Averages can hide unhappy key stakeholders: contact them and find out why
A stakeholder's behavior changes (petitions, public criticism, new alliances) Reclassify them and change the engagement approach (for example from "keep informed" to "manage closely")
A change alters who is affected or how much Re-analyze the stakeholders and reassess engagement levels before notifying anyone
What the customer approved (samples, prototype) differs from what is being built (drawings, specification) Meet the customer to reconcile the two, agree which governs and document it, before changing production
Internal users and external customers want conflicting things Validate a balanced design with both groups; do not simply favor the group you see daily

8Sponsor, Customer, Product Owner and End Users

  • Sponsor (glossary): provides resources and support and is accountable for enabling success. Product owner (glossary): responsible for maximizing the value of the product and accountable for the end product.
  • Sponsor, customer (internal or external) and product owner give decision leadership outside the project management team's authority: they communicate vision, goals and expectations, facilitate executive-level decisions, help secure resources, advocate for the team, and remove obstacles beyond the PM's authority. They are also critical for sustainability and ESG goals.
  • Their involvement increases the likelihood of success; their absence can hurt the project.
  • End users and other key stakeholders: engage in continuous dialogue to capture feedback throughout the life cycle; use iterative verification and validation; prioritizing end-user satisfaction reduces the risk of delivering something that does not meet expected utility.
  • Solicit and manage feedback (Standard §2.4.2) matters even more in adaptive and hybrid work, where teams are exploring the product in increments.

9Predictive vs Agile vs Hybrid

Predictive Agile / adaptive Hybrid
Identification Mostly up front; formal register; refreshed at phase gates and big changes Continuous; whole team and product owner; stakeholders can appear at any iteration Up front for contractual/governance stakeholders, continuous for product users
Engagement mechanisms Stakeholder engagement plan, scheduled meetings, status reports, steering committee, formal change control Product owner as customer voice, sprint/iteration review (demo plus feedback), backlog refinement, retrospectives, daily coordination meetings, information radiators, customer talks and tests Governance reviews at milestones plus iterative reviews of increments
Feedback rhythm At milestones and gates; formal acceptance Every iteration; continuous Both
Expectation management Baselined scope; changes via change control Backlog reprioritized each iteration; expectations refreshed by working increments Baseline for fixed elements, backlog for the rest
Typical failure Stakeholders surprised at the end One-way demos with no feedback time; radiators placed where stakeholders never look; absent product owner Unclear who decides what

10Tailoring Considerations (PMBOK 8 §2.5.3)

  • Organizational culture: flat organizations rely on open, informal channels; hierarchical ones use formal approaches.
  • Product: interactive/incremental products bring their own engagement events (product reviews, planning sessions, retrospectives).
  • AI and LLMs: decide per project when AI should assist (e.g., drafting communications for sponsor, team, vendors); apply security and ethics measures and involve the cybersecurity team to confirm the risk is acceptable.
  • Size and complexity: many stakeholders need a more sophisticated communications plan than a small project with few channels.
  • PMBOK 8 examples: (1) agile project: continuous feedback on features, daily coordination, real-time collaboration platforms; (2) large ERP rollout: biweekly newsletters and monthly town halls to align hierarchical levels; (3) medium global project: multilingual updates and monthly virtual forums.

11Interactions With Other Domains and Checking Results

  • Scope / planning / acceptance: stakeholders define and prioritize requirements and set acceptance and quality criteria.
  • Risk: stakeholders are key sources of risk information; missing the right stakeholders (or not updating the list) raises risk.
  • Governance: the domain depends on skills for engaging governance bodies and organizational leaders. Finance: stakeholders help set budgets, make funding decisions and oversee financial controls.
Outcome How to check
Stakeholder engagement is maintained Interviews or surveys; periodic alignment on objectives; indicators such as Net Promoter Score
Risk responses identified and implemented Review issue log, risk register and stakeholder register
Stakeholder agreement with project objectives Number of change requests to requirements; feedback on increments
Communications management is performed Review the communications plan periodically and tailor it
Plans integrate suppliers' perspectives Align the project management plan with the vendor's way of working

12Exam Traps and What PMI Expects

  1. First move with a disengaged, resistant or unhappy stakeholder is to understand, not to escalate. Talk to them, compare current vs desired engagement, revisit the engagement plan. Escalating, replacing or ignoring comes later (or never).
  2. Stakeholder identification never ends. A late-discovered influential stakeholder is engaged now, and the register and plan are updated; do not wait for the next gate.
  3. A register entry is not engagement. Classification must turn into planned actions.
  4. Engagement plan ≠ communications plan. The first is about engagement strategy, the second about information flow.
  5. Prioritize, but do not ignore. Not every request deserves equal attention; low-power stakeholders (regulators, communities) can still matter.
  6. Conflicting stakeholder demands: bring them together, align on project objectives and value, escalate through governance only if beyond your authority. Never silently pick a side or favor the highest rank.
  7. Expectations must be explicit and documented (assumptions, constraints, success and acceptance criteria) before baselining; new asks go through change control.
  8. Following the plan is not the same as satisfied stakeholders. If their expectations were not met, engage and respond rather than defend the paperwork.
  9. Sponsor: an active sponsor is critical. If they are disengaged, meet them to clarify needs and the decisions you need; do not bypass them.
  10. Agile: build feedback into reviews; make progress visible where stakeholders actually look; keep the product owner available. Do not wait for release to learn what stakeholders think.
  11. Honesty: share bad news early and factually; never spin or hide it (Code of Ethics: honesty, fairness).
  12. Pick the channel to fit the stakeholder (virtual teams: collaboration tools with clear documentation), not one channel for everyone.
  13. Small signals matter. Informal remarks, falling attendance, petitions or silence call for a direct conversation and a fresh look at classification; do not wait for a pattern or a formal complaint, and do not rely on averages.

13Exam Q&A

13.1 Scenario questions (choose the best answer)

S1A neighbor of the worksite, who is not directly affected by the construction, has started a petition because she believes the noise will harm local children. The team says she is not a stakeholder. How should the project manager respond?

  • AAsk the municipality to deal with the petition on the project's behalf
  • BAgree, because only people with a legal or contractual link to the project are stakeholders
  • CTreat her as a stakeholder, since perceived impact counts, and engage her
  • DAdd her to the register but contact her only after the work is complete
Show the answer

Answer: C. A stakeholder is anyone who may affect, be affected by or perceive itself to be affected by the project, and low power never means ignoring someone. Excluding her, deferring contact or passing the issue on leaves a potentially influential concern unaddressed.

S2The stakeholder engagement plan lists strategies for supporters only, and the neutral and resistant groups are not mentioned. What should the project manager do?

  • AKeep the focus on supporters, because they are the ones who will help the project succeed
  • BExtend the analysis and plan to cover supporters, neutral and resistant stakeholders alike
  • CAsk the sponsor to deal with the resistant stakeholders directly and in private
  • DLeave the resistant stakeholders until they raise a formal objection to the project
Show the answer

Answer: B. Stakeholders may be supportive, neutral or opponents, and effective engagement covers all three groups rather than only the friendly ones. Concentrating on supporters, waiting for objections or handing the issue to the sponsor leaves resistance unmanaged.

S3The sponsor of a product has missed the last three sprint reviews, and decisions on priorities are waiting. What should the project manager do?

  • AMake the pending decisions personally so that the team is not held up any longer
  • BMeet the sponsor to explain the need and agree a realistic way to stay involved
  • CSend the sponsor longer written reports and wait for a reply
  • DAsk the steering committee to replace the sponsor immediately
Show the answer

Answer: B. An active sponsor is a critical success factor, so the project manager engages the sponsor directly, makes the cost of absence visible and agrees a workable level of involvement. Deciding alone, seeking a replacement or sending longer reports does not restore that engagement.

S4Three parties call for attention. A regulator has authority, a legitimate claim and an inspection deadline next week; a supplier has a legitimate claim only; an executive has power but no current interest. Who gets the most immediate attention under the salience model?

  • AThe regulator, which combines power, legitimacy and urgency
  • BThe supplier, because legitimacy is the strongest of the three attributes
  • CAll three equally, since the model gives no way of ranking them
  • DThe executive, because power on its own outranks every other attribute
Show the answer

Answer: A. The salience model classes stakeholders by power, urgency and legitimacy, and the party holding all three ranks highest. A single attribute, as with the supplier or the executive, carries less weight, and the model exists precisely to rank relative importance.

S5The chief financial officer has high power but low interest in the agile program, and the daily updates sent by the project manager have prompted a complaint about overload. Which strategy fits this stakeholder?

  • AKeep satisfied by consulting on key financial decisions without overloading with detail
  • BKeep informed by sending even more frequent and detailed updates to the officer
  • CManage closely by involving the officer in all of the project's decisions
  • DMonitor with minimal effort and update the officer only at project closure
Show the answer

Answer: A. A stakeholder with high power and low interest is kept satisfied: consulted on the decisions that matter without being swamped. Managing closely or sending more updates adds to the overload, and monitoring only ignores the power the officer holds.

S6On the engagement assessment matrix, the sponsor is currently neutral but needs to be leading, while the quality lead is supportive and needs to be supportive. Where should the project manager focus effort first?

  • AOn neither, because neutral and supportive are both acceptable levels
  • BOn both equally, because every stakeholder should be brought to the leading level
  • COn the quality lead, because supportive stakeholders are easily lost
  • DOn the sponsor, because the gap between current and desired engagement is largest
Show the answer

Answer: D. The gap between current and desired engagement directs the effort, and the sponsor's two-level gap is the largest while the quality lead already sits at the desired level. Desired levels are set by what the project needs, not by a uniform target.

S7The project has a communications management plan listing who receives which reports and when, yet several key stakeholders remain resistant. What is missing?

  • AA risk register entry for each resistant stakeholder without further actions
  • BA stakeholder engagement plan defining desired engagement levels and how to reach them
  • CA longer distribution list for each of the reports in the communications plan
  • DA more detailed report schedule showing the exact date of every update
Show the answer

Answer: B. The communications plan says what information goes to whom, while the stakeholder engagement plan answers how each stakeholder is moved to the engagement level the project needs. More distribution, finer schedules or bare risk entries do not supply those strategies.

S8The project manager needs a peer department to change its report format for the project but has no authority over that department. Which approach is most likely to succeed?

  • AOffer the department's manager a personal favor in return for cooperation
  • BLearn what matters to the department and persuade by showing mutual benefit
  • CSend the department the new template and proceed unless it objects
  • DCite the sponsor's priority and instruct the department to comply by Friday
Show the answer

Answer: B. With no direct authority, the project manager influences through persuasion, active listening and an understanding of the other side's interests, while maintaining mutual trust. Commanding, assuming silence means consent or trading personal favors damages trust or ethics.

S9The project manager notices that executives often change their positions after talking with the CEO's chief of staff, who holds no formal authority over the project. What should the project manager do?

  • ARecognize the informal influence and build a relationship with the chief of staff
  • BAsk the executives to stop discussing any project matters with the chief of staff
  • CIgnore the chief of staff, since no formal authority exists over the project
  • DReport the chief of staff to the sponsor for interfering with the project
Show the answer

Answer: A. Political awareness means recognizing informal as well as formal power relationships and communicating with those who hold influence. Ignoring, restricting or reporting the chief of staff leaves a major channel of influence unmanaged.

S10In a sprint review, a stakeholder raises his voice and accuses the team of ignoring his requirements. What should the project manager do?

  • AAsk him to leave the meeting until he can speak calmly to the team
  • BDefend the team's record point by point in front of everyone present
  • CStay calm, acknowledge his frustration and talk privately afterward
  • DPostpone the review and send him a summary of the requirements log
Show the answer

Answer: C. Emotional intelligence means recognizing and managing your own emotions and those of others; acknowledging the frustration and moving the discussion to a private, collaborative setting reduces tension. Expelling him, arguing publicly or simply postponing escalates or avoids the issue.

S11A new scrum master asks the project manager for the answer to a facilitation problem. The project manager would prefer that she develops her own judgment. Which approach fits best?

  • ACoaching, by asking questions that help her find the solution herself
  • BMentoring, by telling her exactly how the project manager would handle it
  • CDirecting, by giving her a written procedure to follow every time
  • DDelegating, by asking another team member to solve the problem for her
Show the answer

Answer: A. Coaching helps a person find the solution on their own by asking the right questions, whereas mentoring shares knowledge and experience over a longer relationship. Telling, prescribing or handing the problem to someone else does not build her own judgment.

S12A steering committee has postponed a decision on a vendor change for a hybrid program three times, saying the options are unclear. What should the project manager do?

  • AMake the decision personally, since the committee has repeatedly shown it cannot decide
  • BSchedule a longer committee meeting so that every member can speak
  • CPrepare a decision paper with options, data and a recommendation, and guide the session
  • DSend the committee the full project file and ask for a decision by email
Show the answer

Answer: C. Timely stakeholder decisions come from solid supporting material, with options, data and a recommendation, and from guiding the decision process. Deciding alone, sending everything or simply allowing more talking time does not make the choice clear.

S13The stakeholder register lists only internal departments, because vendors are covered by contracts, and a vendor's late input has now delayed a milestone. What should the project manager do?

  • AAsk the procurement department to manage all vendor communication alone
  • BLeave the register unchanged and enforce the contract's delivery clauses
  • CReplace the vendor whose input arrived late with a different supplier
  • DAdd the vendors as stakeholders and plan how to engage them
Show the answer

Answer: D. Vendors and suppliers are stakeholders wherever external resources are used, so they are identified, analyzed and engaged, with contract terms as one tool among others. Relying on the contract alone, replacing the vendor or delegating everything to procurement misses the engagement.

S14A stakeholder on a global sprint-planning call keeps repeating the same concern, and the project manager is not sure it has been understood. Which technique helps most?

  • AAsk the stakeholder to submit the concern in writing for the record
  • BPromise to look into the concern and follow up with a detailed email
  • CSummarize the project's position and move on to the next agenda item
  • DActive listening: paraphrase the concern and confirm understanding
Show the answer

Answer: D. Active listening means acknowledging, clarifying and confirming what was said so that the concern is truly understood, which matters most in global settings. Restating the project's position, deferring to email or demanding a written submission does not confirm understanding.

S15While reviewing the contract, the project manager finds obligations toward an inspection body that does not appear in the stakeholder register. What should the project manager do?

  • ANotify the inspection body only when the deliverable is ready for inspection
  • BLeave it out, since the contract rather than the register governs the obligation
  • CAdd it to the register, analyze its needs and influence, and plan how to engage it
  • DAsk the legal department to manage all contact with the inspection body
Show the answer

Answer: C. Stakeholders are found in documents such as contracts and agreements, and identification is continuous, which also acts as a risk management strategy. Leaving the body out, contacting it late or delegating the relationship skips analysis and engagement planning.

S16The project manager notices that most of the pressure on her scope comes from managers of other projects that share her specialists. Which direction of influence does this describe?

  • ADownward, because the pressure comes from the members of the project team
  • BSideward, because the pressure comes from peers outside the project
  • COutward, because the pressure comes from organizations outside the company
  • DUpward, because the pressure comes from the organization's senior management
Show the answer

Answer: B. Directions of influence classify stakeholders as upward (senior management), downward (the team), outward (outside the organization) and sideward (peers), and managers of other projects in the same organization are peers.

S17A budget cut forces the product team to drop a feature from the backlog, and the project manager is tempted to decide alone to spare the team the stress. What is the better approach?

  • ADecide alone and announce the result, since leaders must carry the difficult decisions
  • BAsk the sponsor to choose the feature to drop and inform the team afterward
  • CLet the team vote anonymously and apply the result without any review
  • DInvolve the team, since hard-decision recommendations come from those doing the work
Show the answer

Answer: D. Team members are critical stakeholders, and the work and the recommendations for hard decisions come from them, so they are involved in the decision. Deciding alone, passing the choice upward or applying an unreviewed vote bypasses their expertise or the manager's accountability.

13.2 Recall Q&As

R1How does PMBOK 8 define a stakeholder?

Show the answer

An individual, group or organization that may affect, be affected by, or perceive itself to be affected by a decision, activity or outcome of a portfolio, program or project.

R2Name the four engagement processes and their focus areas.

Show the answer

Identify Stakeholders (Initiating); Plan Stakeholder Engagement (Planning); Manage Stakeholder Engagement (Executing); Monitor Stakeholder Engagement (Monitoring & Controlling).

R3What are the five engagement levels?

Show the answer

Unaware, Resistant, Neutral, Supportive, Leading.

R4What do C and D mean in the assessment matrix, and what do you do with the gap?

Show the answer

C is current engagement, D is desired. The gap directs the level of communication and engagement effort; closing it is an essential element of monitoring.

R5List the five stakes a stakeholder can hold.

Show the answer

Interest, rights (legal or moral), ownership, knowledge, contribution.

R6What does the stakeholder register contain?

Show the answer

Identification information, assessment information (requirements, expectations, influence potential, phase of most influence) and classification (internal/external, power/interest and similar models, direction of influence).

R7What are the four directions of influence?

Show the answer

Upward (senior management, sponsor, steering committee), downward (team and specialists), outward (outside groups such as suppliers, regulators, end users), sideward (peers competing for or sharing resources).

R8Which quadrant is "keep satisfied"?

Show the answer

High power, low interest. (High/high = manage closely; low power/high interest = keep informed; low/low = monitor.)

R9What is the difference between coaching and mentoring?

Show the answer

Coaching helps someone solve a specific problem themselves by asking the right questions and is goal-oriented. Mentoring is a long-term relationship of sharing knowledge, skills and experience. Both are one-to-one.

R10What is the key benefit of Manage Stakeholder Engagement?

Show the answer

Increasing support and minimizing resistance.

R11What attributes does the salience model use?

Show the answer

Power, urgency and legitimacy (proximity replaces legitimacy in the team-level adaptation).

R12Why is continuous stakeholder identification described as a risk strategy?

Show the answer

Because stakeholders change and unidentified or ignored stakeholders add uncertainty; refreshing the list as the environment evolves reduces surprises.
